Support MP/ML: 56/70. The composite: sections Nepenthoidea, Decipientia, Franchetiana, Sinarisaema and Pistillata. Pistillata (A. lobatum through A. sikokianum) is a recent, mostly Japanese radiation — many of its species share identical plastid sequences, so much of the clade is drawn unresolved. A. triphyllum sits here too: its split from Asian A. amurense is the fossil-calibrated 18-My Beringian crossing the genus's whole clock hangs on.

children.speciesTierSource: Ohi-Toma, Wu, Murata & Murata (2016), "An updated genus-wide phylogenetic analysis of Arisaema (Araceae) with reference to sections", Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society 182: 100-114, Figs 1-3; dates on the cards are Renner, Zhang & Murata (2004), American Journal of Botany 91(6): 881-888
children.speciesTierNote: No dated species-level tree exists for Arisaema, so this tier shows grouping, not time — Renner, Zhang & Murata (2004)'s fossil-calibrated clock (an 18-My A. triphyllum-like infructescence from Spokane) puts the genus's origin possibly in the Oligocene, with the root constrained to at most 60 My, and dates the intercontinental splits quoted on the clade cards. The tier itself is Ohi-Toma et al. (2016): more than 150 accessions, four plastid non-coding regions, MP and ML — eight major clades and one unique branch (I-IX) whose relationships to each other are largely an unresolved polytomy, listed here in the study's drawn order. The sections of the Murata system are named on every species row; the study's own treatment recognises 15, resurrecting Fimbriata and moving A. schimperianum into section Arisaema. Most sections map cleanly onto clades — the exceptions are said so on their cards. 157 figure tips collapse to 124 species-level rows here; many Japanese Pistillata species share identical plastid sequences.

chron.note: From the Philodendron study (Canal et al. 2019), not the family chronogram the rest of this view is drawn from. Its stem is shared with Adelonema, its sister genus. Canal et al. (2018) date the same nodes at 25.53 / 22.10 Ma on the same three secondary calibrations with 48 fewer taxa, and at 21.55 / 18.61 Ma when a Montrichardia fossil is added instead - the ages are not strictly comparable with the genera around them.

Both numbers are given. ⚠ The two studies disagree about which subgenus branches first, and both mark that node as too weakly supported to date: 2018 has subgenus Philodendron splitting off first (pp 0.37), 2019 has Pteromischum (pp 0.27). children.speciesTierNote: No PUBLISHED dated tree exists for Anthurium (even 2026 phylogenomics calls calibration future work), so this tier shows grouping, not time — but Carlsen's 2011 dissertation dated it once, unpublished (r8s, Pothoideae crown fixed at 86 Mya): genus crown ~27.2 Mya (Late Oligocene), the core radiation (its Clade B) ~8.9 Mya, and nearly all species-level diversification between ~12 Mya and the Holocene. Its clade ages are quoted on the clade cards; its clade NUMBERS differ from the 2019 numbering used here, so every match was made by membership, never by number. The supported units are the study's numbered clades; the classical sections growers know are named on every species row — and 10 of the 15 sections tested are NOT natural groups. Clade A is the genus's earliest divergent lineage; everything else forms the strongly supported Clade B (99/100/1.00), whose internal backbone is largely unresolved — the numbered clades are listed in the study's own drawn order.

intro: This tree shows how the roughly 150 accepted genera of the arum family are grouped: first into subfamilies, then into tribes, and finally into the genera themselves.

Its backbone comes from The Genera of Araceae (Mayo, Bogner and Boyce, Kew, 1997), still the only work that places every genus in a tribe. Where later research has changed that picture, the tree follows the later research.

currentWith.heading: Brought up to date with the 2022 phylogenomic study
currentWith.body: The most recent family-wide study (Haigh and colleagues, 2022, American Journal of Botany) sequenced 128 species across 111 genera. Its conclusions are applied here, not just noted:
applied: Calla now sits inside Aroideae. The old subfamily Calloideae is not used.
Zamioculcadoideae is treated as part of Aroideae.
The duckweeds are included as subfamily Lemnoideae — they were still a separate family in 1997.
Lasioideae is divided into two tribes, Lasieae and Dracontieae.
The tribe Aglaonemateae holds Aglaonema and Boycea.
unresolved: Where subfamily Lasioideae attaches to the rest of the family is still unsettled.
The positions of Montrichardia, Zantedeschia and Anchomanes are only moderately supported.

uncertainty.heading: Why some branches are dashed
uncertainty.body: A dashed branch means the genus was named, revived or moved after 1997 and no study we hold places it in a tribe outright. Its position is our best reading of the literature rather than a published conclusion, and it is drawn differently so you can tell the two apart. Every other genus here sits where a named source puts it.

counts.heading: Where the numbers come from
counts.body: Species totals follow Kew's Plants of the World Online and count formally described species. Aroidpedia's own pages often list more, because the archive covers plants that have not been described yet.

reading.heading: Reading the tree
reading.body: Colour marks the level: family, subfamily, tribe, genus. A branch takes the colour of whatever it leads to, so you can follow a lineage down by shade alone. Selecting a genus lights its whole line back to the family.

taxa.method: Stem and crown ages for Aroidpedia's own subfamilies, tribes and genera, read off Nauheimer, Metzler & Renner (2012). Their Fig. S2 chronogram was rebuilt from the vector strokes in the supplement PDF - 146 tip branches and 144 internal branches, exactly the 2T-2 a binary tree of 146 tips must have - so the topology is the drawing itself rather than a reading of it. Node numbers were assigned from the printed numerals and Table S5's ages together (median numeral distance 5.6 pt, median age residual 0.07 Ma), and the result reproduces all nine crown-group labels Table S5 states, all twelve nodes the paper names in prose, and exactly the four genera the paper calls polyphyletic. Every age here is Table S5's number, never a measurement off the figure. STEM is the split from the sampled sister lineage and CROWN the oldest split inside the taxon, so a crown exists only where two or more species were sampled; both are conditioned on the study's 132-taxon sample and are minimum ages for the taxon as circumscribed today. A taxon whose sampled species do not form a clade in this tree carries mono:false and its MRCA instead of a date - that is a finding, not a gap. Note Aroideae: the study kept Zamioculcadoideae separate, so its Aroideae is node 41 (82.1); this tree follows Haigh et al. (2022) in holding Zamioculcadeae and Stylochaetoneae inside Aroideae, which makes the crown node 38 (87.0). SUPERSEDES metadata.chronology.tribes, whose node identities came from reading Fig. 3 by eye: three of them pointed one node off (Cryptocoryneae/Schismatoglottideae stem is 37.2 at node 97, not 45.2 at node 96; Areae 30.3 is the stem, not the crown; the Arisaema lineage stem is node 73 at 31.7, not node 71 at 34.7). Readers on 1.11.0 or later should use taxa and ignore tribes. 1.12.0: two synonymies applied before the tips were mapped - Landoltia is Spirodela, and Pseudodracontium is Amorphophallus (Claudel et al. 2017, followed by POWO). Both were separate tips in the study, so folding them changes what those two genera are: Spirodela and Amorphophallus each gain a sampled tip, and Amorphophallus no longer has a sister genus to take a stem age from.
